readerTitle: Why four gas stations share one corner
caseNote: 실제 관찰 (주유소 군집, 매장 매출 의존) + 가상 적용 (주유소 입지, 타이어 가게, 배관 서비스)
insight: 같은 상품을 파는 경쟁자 옆에 서면 가격으로는 이길 수 없으니, 돈은 같이 사 가는 상품(보완재)에서 번다.
misconception: 경쟁자 바로 옆에 가게를 내면 손님을 나눠 먹으니 무조건 손해다.

sources.text: 미국 편의점협회(NACS) 업계 자료: 연료 마진은 얇고 매장 상품 판매가 이익에서 큰 비중을 차지한다는 일반적 관찰
주유소·타이어 가게·배관 서비스 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 연료 마진이 얇고 매장 판매가 이익의 큰 몫이라는 내용은 NACS 자료로 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 구체적 수치를 넣지 않고 일반적 표현으로만 썼습니다.
주유소가 교차로에 몰리는 현상과 인접 주유소 가격이 몇 센트 안에서 비슷하다는 서술은 일반적 관찰로 썼습니다. 특정 연구 수치를 인용하지 않았습니다.
가격 담합 관련 법률 언급은 가이드 범위 밖이라 '따라 맞추기'와 '합의'를 구분하는 일반적 문장만 남겼습니다.

cards.title: Why four gas stations share one corner
body: Drive to a busy crossroads. There's often a station on two, three, even four corners. Their price signs sit within a few cents of each other.
Then drive a mile down a quiet road. Nothing. Why would anyone build right next to a rival selling the exact same thing?

image.label: Four gas stations on the corners of one intersection
image.brief: 위에서 내려다본 교차로. 네 모퉁이에 각각 주유소, 가격 간판 숫자가 거의 같음(예: 3.49, 3.49, 3.51, 3.48). 멀리 한적한 도로는 비어 있음. 실제 정유사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Where do you build your station?
body: You're opening a gas station. Site A sits at a busy junction with three rivals already there. Site B is on a quieter road with no station for miles, and rent is cheaper.

options.text: Site B. No rivals means you can charge more
options.feedback: You'd have some pricing room, but far fewer cars pass by. Drivers rarely detour for gas, so a small local edge can't make up for missing traffic.

options.text: Site A, and win drivers with the lowest price on the corner
options.feedback: You'd get the traffic, but rivals can match a sign change within hours. Gas is a commodity, so a price lead rarely lasts and just thins everyone's margin.

options.text: Site A, matching rivals on fuel and earning on the shop, coffee and car wash
options.feedback: You go where the cars are, accept the market price on fuel, and make money on things drivers buy alongside it. The next cards show why.

cards.title: Customers come to the corner, not to you.
body: Drivers don't plan a trip for gas. They fill up on routes they already drive, so demand piles up where the traffic is.
A busy junction also becomes known as *the place to get gas*. Each extra station makes the corner a surer bet for drivers, which brings more cars for everyone.
Being alone on a quiet road means less competition, but also far fewer customers to compete for.

cards.title: On fuel, the corner sets your price.
body: Gas is a **commodity**: one station's regular unleaded works the same as the next. When products are interchangeable, the market sets the price and each seller mostly follows it.

On the corner, your rivals are near-perfect **substitutes**, and their prices are on giant signs. Charge ten cents more and drivers turn across the street. Charge ten cents less and rivals match by evening.
So clustering doesn't give you pricing power. It gives you traffic, at the market price.

image.label: Price signs from four stations nearly identical
image.brief: 네 개의 주유소 가격 간판을 나란히 배치한 인포그래픽. 숫자가 거의 같고, 한 간판만 10센트 높게 표시된 쪽으로 차들이 등을 돌리는 화살표. 로고 없음.

cards.title: The money is inside the shop.
body: Drivers who stop for fuel also buy coffee, snacks, drinks and car washes. These are **complements**: products bought together with the main one.
Industry groups for convenience retailers report that fuel margins are usually thin, and that in-store sales earn a large share of a station's profit.
That explains the corner. Fuel brings the cars. Complements, where prices are less compared, pay the bills.
cards.softwareNote: Comparison sites turn many digital products into commodities too. Hosting or basic storage plans sit side by side, so firms often price the core near rivals and earn on add-ons like support, backups or extra features.

cards.title: A tire shop on auto row.
body: Your city has an "auto row" with four tire shops selling the same major tire brands. You can open there or in a quiet suburb with no rival nearby.

options.text: Open on auto row and promise the lowest tire prices
options.feedback: Same brands make your tires substitutes for theirs. They'll match, and you'll all earn less on a commodity.

options.text: Open on auto row, price tires at market, and earn on alignment, seasonal storage and fast fitting
options.feedback: Shoppers come to auto row to compare, so you get the traffic. Complements like storage and alignment are where your margin lives.

options.text: Open in the suburb and charge a bit more
options.feedback: Nearby customers may pay for convenience, but many tire buyers head to where they can compare. Fine if local demand is big enough.

cards.title: Clustering only pays under some conditions.
list: **Customers must gather in one place.** If they search online first, the corner matters less.
**Complements must be real.** A cluster with nothing extra to sell is just a price fight.
**Matching is not agreeing.** Following a rival's posted price is normal. Coordinating prices with rivals is a different matter.
cards.callout: Check where customers actually decide before you follow the crowd.

cards.title: A plumber on a booking app.
body: You run a plumbing business. On a local booking app, "drain clearing" shows twelve plumbers in a list, each with a price. Yours sits in the middle.

options.text: Cut your drain price to the lowest on the list
options.feedback: On the list, drain clearing looks like a commodity, and every rival is a substitute one tap away. Others can cut too, and the race goes to zero.

options.text: Stay near the typical price and offer an annual plumbing check after each job
options.feedback: The app is your busy corner: it brings the customers. The yearly check is a complement that turns one cheap job into steady, less compared work.

options.text: Leave the app and rely on word of mouth
options.feedback: You escape the price list, but you also leave the place where customers gather. Works only if referrals already fill your week.

cards.title: Go where customers gather. Earn on what they buy alongside.
body: Recap: **commodities** explain why prices on the corner converge, **substitutes** explain why you can't stand apart on price, and **complements** explain where the profit comes from.
**Try it today:** name the spot, real or online, where customers compare you with rivals. List one complement you could sell there.
